ranked.name: Terminal-Bench 4.0 (harbor-framework/terminal-bench @ v4.0.0)
ranked.why: This is the best match on every weighted criterion. (1) Length and headroom: I parsed all 66 v4.0.0 task.toml files. The expert-estimate median is 4.0 h, 52 of 66 tasks fall in the 1-8 h band, and every task has a flat 28,800 s agent timeout (https://github.com/harbor-framework/terminal-bench/tree/v4.0.0/tasks; https://www.tbench.ai/news/terminal-bench-4-0). Claude Code + Sonnet 5.5 scores 61.8% ±2.9 (Snorkel, https://snorkel.ai/leaderboard/terminal-bench-4-0/). Vals reports Sonnet 5.5 at 64.14% with an average of 1h22m and $16.51 per task (mini-swe-agent, avg@3, https://vals.ai/benchmarks/terminal-bench-4), so the baseline is mid-range and a typical run fits the 30-90 min budget. (2) Hidden objective scoring: all 66 tasks set verifier environment_mode="separate" (my count from the task.toml files), and the leaderboard gives no partial credit (Vals). (3) arm64: no task.toml sets docker_image, so Harbor builds locally from Dockerfiles. The shortlisted bases are multi-arch: python:3.x-slim, ubuntu:24.04, node, oven/bun. No task sets network_mode, so the default is public and Harbor's macOS nftables bugs do not apply. (4)/(5) Harbor's claude-code agent accepts CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN with CLAUDE_FORCE_OAUTH=1; its error message tells you to run `claude setup-token` (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/harbor-framework/harbor/main/src/harbor/agents/installed/claude_code.py). The source also shows `--skill` copying the skill dir into $CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR/skills (https://docs.harborframework.com/jobs/skills). The treatment arm is therefore just `--skill .claude/skills/horizon`, and both arms share the same agent and token. Bonus: --resume-trajectory and multi-step tasks give a hook for interrupt/resume (https://docs.harborframework.com/tasks/multi-step). Conflicts I resolved: the v4.0.0 GitHub release is dated 2026-08-26 and v3.0.0 (74 tasks) 2026-07-23 (https://api.github.com/repos/harbor-framework/terminal-bench/releases). Snorkel's token figures are per model: Opus 5.5 used 8.0B tokens / $4.7k and Sonnet 5.5 19.4B / $7.3k for the full 66-task run, so both searchers' numbers were right. Snorkel lists Sonnet 5.5's release as 2026-09-28.
ranked.risks: Five tasks are open-flagged as not multi-platform (#1802 coq-block-bound, #1803 hof-topology-interpenetration, #1804 math-eval-grader, #1805 gsea-proteomics, #1806 wdm-design; all 2026-08-26), and #1601 records a task that was silently unsolvable on arm64 (https://github.com/harbor-framework/terminal-bench/issues?q=is%3Aissue+amd64). Harbor #2758 (open): an arm64/x86 mismatch yields reward 0 that is indistinguishable from an agent failure, so every task must be oracle-validated on the M4 (https://github.com/harbor-framework/harbor/issues/2758). Resources: memory requests are 4/8/16/32 GB for 35/22/8/1 tasks, and 3 tasks need a GPU. Docker Desktop's VM defaults to 50% of host RAM, so raise it above 8 GB and run n_concurrent=1. Binary rewards at n=10 give low statistical power. Some tasks are non-coding (FreeCAD, science, media). Some shortlisted bases (ubuntu:24.04, node:*-slim) may lack python3, which horizon's scripts need. Contamination: the public repo has had solution/ directories and a canary GUID since 2026-07-23, before Sonnet 5.5 shipped on 2026-09-28. The blog says 2 tasks were removed for public solutions. Usage: 1-1.5 h of Sonnet 5.5 per trial, so 20 trials is roughly $330 API-equivalent and 100 trials roughly $1.65k.
key_facts_to_verify: At least 10-15 shortlisted CPU tasks build natively on arm64 and score reward=1 with `harbor run -p tasks/<t> -a oracle --force-build` on the M4. Harbor #2758 makes arm64 failures look like agent failures, and 5 TB4 tasks are already flagged amd64-only (#1802-#1806).

Harbor's claude-code agent runs on the subscription via CLAUDE_FORCE_OAUTH=1 + CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN from `claude setup-token` (the code path is verified in claude_code.py), and the plan's usage limits tolerate about 20 trials of about 1-1.5 h of Sonnet 5.5 each (Vals: 1h22m, $16.51/task; Snorkel full run: 19.4B tokens).

The plain Claude Code + Sonnet 5.5 baseline on the chosen subset lands roughly between 20% and 80% (61.8% overall on Snorkel, 64.14% on Vals). If the chosen tasks are all-pass or all-fail for the baseline, no horizon effect can show.

horizon's scripts can run inside each task container: python3 is present (ubuntu:24.04 and node:*-slim bases may not ship it), `--skill` copies the scripts/ and references/ subdirs (Harbor does `cp -r <skills_dir>/*`), and the horizon ledger writes to the container rather than the host repo.
Agent network stays public by default (no network_mode in any v4.0.0 task.toml, which I verified), so Harbor macOS issues #2593 and #2527 do not block runs.
Contamination: whether Sonnet 5.5's training data included TB3/TB4 public solution/ dirs. If it did, the baseline is inflated and headroom shrinks.
ranked.setup_effort: Low to medium. `uv tool install harbor` (0.24.0, https://pypi.org/pypi/harbor/json), start Docker Desktop and raise its VM memory to about 12 GB, run `claude setup-token`, then check out tag v4.0.0 and oracle-validate about 15 tasks with --force-build. Images build locally, so expect 10-30 min of building per task the first time. Both arms: `-a claude-code -m anthropic/<sonnet-5.5> --agent-timeout-multiplier 0.1875` (90 min) or 0.25 (2 h); the treatment arm adds `--skill .claude/skills/horizon`. About half a day before any model spend.
ranked.pilot_subset_idea: Start from the 45 tasks I computed that have no GPU, ≤8 CPU, ≤8 GB, a 1-8 h expert estimate, and are not in #1802-1806. Drop the compose/multi-container ones (e.g. payments-pipeline-fix). Prefer Software/ML/Operations tasks with 2-8 h estimates: mvcc-lsm-compaction (4 h), wal-recovery-ordering (6 h), session-window-debug (8 h), vf2-speedup-networkx (4 h), embedding-drift-monitor (5 h), mp-checkpoint-consolidation (6 h), risk-scorer-replay (4 h), production-planning (4 h), cargo-flight-dispatch (2.5 h), react-lead-form (5 h), pretrain-shard-corruption (2 h), bun-sourcemap-leak (1.5 h). Keep the first 10 that pass the arm64 oracle. If the Harbor Hub leaderboard exposes per-task Claude Code + Sonnet 5.5 success, prefer tasks at 20-80%. Cap both arms at the same multiplier.

ranked.name: DeepSWE v1.1 (Datacurve)
ranked.why: Best SWE-domain option. It has 113 original long-horizon feature tasks in 91 repos (https://github.com/datacurve-ai/deep-swe; the tasks/ directory lists 113 task dirs plus 4 metadata files). Grading is hidden and program-based: a collect hook writes `git diff <base> HEAD` to model.patch, which is graded in a separate no-network verifier container (verified in task.toml, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/datacurve-ai/deep-swe/main/tasks/bandit-incremental-cache-control/task.toml), and reward.json carries a binary reward plus pass fractions, which gives partial credit for statistical power (README). It is mid-range for Claude: Sonnet 5 [max] 54%±4% at $26.40/task over 268 steps, Opus 5 74%±4%, with no Sonnet 5.5 row (https://deepswe.datacurve.ai/, updated 2026-09-22). Long trajectories leave room for early stopping. Each task needs 2 CPU, 8 GB and a 3 h agent timeout. The dataset is on Harbor Hub (https://hub.harborframework.com/datasets/datacurve/deep-swe-1-1/latest), so stock Harbor's OAuth-capable claude-code agent can be used instead of Pier, whose docs only show ANTHROPIC_API_KEY or ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN (https://github.com/datacurve-ai/pier). Conflicts I resolved: (a) the prebuilt task images are amd64-only. I read the registry manifests for 6 sampled tags (bandit, wasmi, kcp-go, vitest, textual, helm): single-arch, config architecture=amd64, built 2026-06-11. However, each task ships environment/Dockerfile FROM public.ecr.aws/x8v8d7g8/mars-base:latest, which is a multi-arch amd64+arm64 manifest list (verified), so a native arm64 rebuild via --force-build is plausible. (b) The claim that reference solutions are not public is wrong: tasks/<id>/solution/solution.patch is in the public repo (34 KB for bandit-incremental-cache-control).
ranked.risks: Both the agent and verifier set network_mode="no-network". On Docker Desktop, Harbor rejects static no-network (#2593, open, https://github.com/harbor-framework/harbor/issues/2593) and allowlist mode fails because LinuxKit lacks NFT_FIB (#2527, open; the issue says no Docker Desktop upgrade fixes it, https://github.com/harbor-framework/harbor/issues/2527). You would therefore set network to public in local task copies, which departs from the official protocol, and disallow WebFetch/WebSearch. 8 GB per container plus the Docker VM leaves room for only one concurrent task. There are no human-time estimates (the paper says it makes none). The leaderboard is mini-swe-agent, not Claude Code; Claude Code scaffolding lifted Sonnet 5 to 88-93% on SWE-bench Pro V2, so Sonnet 5.5 + Claude Code could approach ceiling here too. Solutions have been public on GitHub since about 2026-07, before Sonnet 5.5. Rebuilding Go/Rust/TS toolchains natively may fail for some repos.
key_facts_to_verify: Task Dockerfiles rebuild natively on arm64 and the oracle (solution.patch) scores reward 1. The prebuilt task images are amd64-only (verified on 6 tags), but mars-base:latest is amd64+arm64 (verified); each repo's dependencies must also build on arm64, otherwise every run is an emulated 8 GB container.

Stock Harbor runs datacurve/deep-swe-1-1 (or `-p deep-swe/tasks`) with `-a claude-code` and the verifier.collect hook that produces /logs/artifacts/model.patch. The official runs used Pier + mini-swe-agent, and Pier documents only API-key or auth-token env vars.
Flipping [agent] and [verifier] network_mode to public in local copies is enough to run on Docker Desktop (#2593 and #2527 are still open) and does not change grading results.
Sonnet 5.5 + Claude Code is not near ceiling on the chosen subset (Sonnet 5 via mini-swe-agent: 54%; Opus 5: 74%).
reward.json pass fractions are populated per task, so partial credit can be used as the primary metric.
Sonnet 5.5 wall-clock per task fits about 90 min (no published duration; Sonnet 5 averaged 268 steps).
ranked.setup_effort: Medium. Clone the repo; for each pilot task, edit network_mode to public, run `harbor run -p deep-swe/tasks/<t> -a oracle --force-build` on the M4, then run both arms with `--agent-timeout-multiplier 0.5`. Raise the Docker Desktop VM to at least 12 GB. Expect a full day to validate about 15 tasks.
ranked.pilot_subset_idea: Start with Python tasks, since pip-based images are the most likely to rebuild cleanly on arm64: bandit-*, httpx-*, textual-*, kombu-*, fastapi-*, narwhals-*, tomlkit-*, sqlite-utils-*, vulture-*, mashumaro-*. Add a few TS/Go tasks once they pass the oracle. Rank by solution.patch size and test count as a length proxy, take the middle-to-upper tercile, skip the very largest, and keep 10 that pass the oracle natively.

ranked.name: Long-Horizon-Terminal-Bench (LHTB)
ranked.why: Purpose-built for our failure mode. It has 46 tasks with a standard 90-minute budget (https://github.com/zli12321/LHTB README; paper average 85.3 min and 9.9M tokens per run, https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.08964). Hidden, deterministic subtask graders give dense partial credit (mean reward 0-1), which gives far more power at n=10 than binary reward. Resources are small (mostly 2 CPU / 4 GB), and expert estimates put 39 of 47 tasks in the 1-8 h band (searcher count). It is Apache-2.0. Uniquely, the bundled Harbor fork has a continue-until-timeout mode: it reruns the agent with only a binary rejection whenever the hidden verifier fails, which in effect is a perfect external gate (README). Run single-shot with stock Harbor for both arms; stock Harbor ignores the flag and runs tasks single-shot (README). You can then use the fork's mode as a ceiling reference to measure how much of a perfect gate's benefit horizon's self-authored gate recovers. Claude baselines (README, July 2026 snapshot, fork harness): Sonnet 5 mean reward 0.497 with 8/46 solved at $60.37/task, Opus 4.8 0.492, Sonnet 4.6 0.373. These are mid-range, not floor.
ranked.risks: Every image is amd64-only. The README tells Apple Silicon users to export DOCKER_DEFAULT_PLATFORM=linux/amd64, so every run is emulated (Rosetta must be enabled in Docker Desktop). That is slower and possibly flaky for scientific-computing tasks, and Harbor PR #2794 (open) reports the arm64 egress sidecar breaking under this setting, although that only matters for non-public network tasks. The README quickstart uses OPENAI_API_KEY/OPENROUTER_API_KEY for Terminus-2; Claude Code through stock Harbor is undocumented and unverified. Published numbers come from the fork's continue-until-timeout loop, so single-shot scores will be lower. task.toml agent timeouts vary from 3,600 to 28,800 s, and Harbor offers only --agent-timeout-multiplier (verified in jobs.py), so a uniform 90-min cap needs per-task configs. Git LFS is required. About $60/task API-equivalent is heavy on a subscription. Tasks were public from 2026-07, before Sonnet 5.5.
key_facts_to_verify: The chosen tasks pass `-a oracle` with reward about 1 under amd64 emulation on the M4 (all images amd64-only), and emulation slowdown leaves the 90-min agent budget usable.
Stock Harbor `-a claude-code` with OAuth loads LHTB task dirs single-shot, and the separate grading environment still isolates the verifier from the agent.

Single-shot Sonnet 5.5 mean reward on the pilot tasks is clearly above 0. Published Claude numbers (Sonnet 5: 0.497) were produced with the fork's verifier-feedback loop, so single-shot will be lower.
A uniform 90-min cap can be enforced per task despite the differing task.toml timeouts, via a per-task config or edited copies, because Harbor exposes only multipliers.
Git LFS assets pull completely, and no grader needs an API key (no API-key env vars in any task.toml, per the searcher).
ranked.setup_effort: Medium. git lfs install/pull, enable Rosetta emulation in Docker Desktop, install stock Harbor, write per-task timeout overrides, and oracle-validate the pilot tasks under emulation. Optionally install the bundled fork (`pip install -e harbor`) in a separate venv to run the oracle-gated reference arm.
ranked.pilot_subset_idea: Pick the 10 tasks that have ≤4 GB memory, a 2-8 h expert estimate and a 3,600-5,400 s timeout, from the SWE, systems/security, scientific computing and professional-workflow categories (avoid the multimodal and game tasks). Prefer tasks where the README's per-model results show partial but not full solves, and drop any that fail the emulated oracle.

ranked.name: FeatureBench (LiberCoders, ICLR 2026)
ranked.why: Large feature tasks (790 lines across about 16 files on average) with hidden F2P/P2P pytest tests and a continuous %Passed metric for partial credit. Claude Code is supported natively via `fb infer` and through a Harbor adapter, and Opus-class resolve rates are low to moderate (https://github.com/LiberCoders/FeatureBench; https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.10975). Dataset v1.1 is from 2026-08.
ranked.risks: I verified on Docker Hub (https://hub.docker.com/v2/repositories/libercoders/) that the images are amd64-only and about 10-12 GB compressed each: flask 10.2 GB, pandas 12.1 GB, sympy 10.6 GB. So 10 tasks is more than 100 GB of disk, with every run emulated. 44 of 200 tasks need a GPU and fail silently with reward 0. Tasks are mined from public repo histories, so contamination is possible. Subscription auth in config.toml is unknown; use Harbor's adapter for OAuth.
ranked.setup_effort: Medium to high: very large amd64 images and emulation.
ranked.pilot_subset_idea: Use the CPU-only 'fast' or 'lite' split and pick mid-size L1 tasks with the smallest images.

ranked.name: SWE-Chain (CUHK-ARISE)
ranked.why: Chained release-level upgrades in which every version step is a natural checkpoint, which suits the interrupt/resume test. Claude Code is supported, and the README explicitly supports CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN, copying local credentials into the sandbox (https://github.com/CUHK-ARISE/SWE-Chain). Claude Code + Opus 4.7 resolves 60.8%, which is mid-range, and target-version tests are run in isolated containers (https://arxiv.org/html/2605.14415v1).
ranked.risks: Targets are famous packages (Flask, Jinja2, pytest, urllib3), so the model may recall the target-version code, and with network access it could pip-download the answer. Whether target tests are hidden is not explicit. Image architecture is unknown. A whole chain takes 3+ h, so use single transitions.
ranked.pilot_subset_idea: Single version transitions with 500-1,300 diff lines from the less-famous packages (conan, PyJWT, xarray), with network blocked.

ranked.name: Terminal-Bench 2.0 / 2.1
ranked.why: The cheapest well-documented pipeline smoke test. It has 89 tasks with expert and junior time estimates (expert median 60 min; about 40 tasks at 1-8 h), small prebuilt images, hidden tests and Harbor claude-code support (https://github.com/harbor-framework/terminal-bench-2; https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.11868). This repo supersedes laude-institute/terminal-bench-2.
ranked.risks: All 89 prebuilt images are amd64-only (per the searcher's Docker Hub check), so they run under emulation. Default timeouts are short (900 s for 48 tasks). Tasks have been public since 2025-11, and the 2.x scores of Opus 4.7 (69.4%) and GPT-5.5 (82%) suggest Sonnet 5.5 may be near ceiling (https://benchlm.ai/md/benchmarks/terminal-bench-2.md). Use it only to debug the Harbor + OAuth + --skill pipeline before spending on TB4.
ranked.pilot_subset_idea: 2-3 tasks from terminal-bench-sample@2.0 to validate plumbing; not for the main comparison.

ranked.name: NL2Repo-Bench
ranked.why: Builds a whole Python library from a natural-language spec, scored by hidden upstream pytest suites with a partial pass rate. The paper documents premature termination and non-finish behavior directly (https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.12730v1).
ranked.risks: The repo documents only OpenHands, so a Claude Code adapter is needed (https://github.com/multimodal-art-projection/NL2RepoBench). Target libraries are public OSS, so memorization is possible. Architecture is unknown. Opus 5 reaches 75% on the aggregator leaderboard (https://benchlm.ai is not the source; see https://benchmarklist.com/benchmarks/nl2repo/), so headroom shrinks for Sonnet 5.5.

ranked.name: LongCLI-Bench
ranked.why: Its profile matches horizon's target exactly: human average of more than 1,000 min, agents stall early at 8.8-30.2 min per attempt, and Claude Code + Opus 4.6 passes 16.7% (F2P step score 50.7%), with hidden F2P/P2P tests and step-level partial credit (https://arxiv.org/html/2602.14337v1).
ranked.risks: The harness is the older TB1-style `tb` CLI, and the README requires LLM_BASE_URL/LLM_API_KEY (https://github.com/finyorko/longcli-bench). Claude Code subscription support is unknown, n=20, and architecture is unknown.
ranked.pilot_subset_idea: All 20 tasks are candidates; pick by step-score mid-range.

ranked.name: SWE-Milestone (DeepCommit-ai)
ranked.why: Dependency-ordered milestones act as natural checkpoints, and the runner auto-resumes interrupted trials (https://github.com/DeepCommit-ai/SWE-Milestone). Isolated evaluation containers support F2P and regression scoring (https://arxiv.org/html/2603.13428).
ranked.risks: Claude Code auth goes through UNIFIED_API_KEY/UNIFIED_BASE_URL (README), so the subscription path is unknown. Milestone resolve rates are 1.3-13.4%, a floor risk. Built from public histories. Architecture and test hiding are unknown.
ranked.pilot_subset_idea: Single milestones that have partial-credit Score.

ranked.name: ImpossibleBench (Impossible-SWEbench)
ranked.why: Not long-horizon, but the most direct cheap probe of horizon's gate behavior under pressure. The tests contradict the spec, so any pass means cheating, and an honest budget-exhausted report is the correct outcome (https://github.com/safety-research/impossiblebench; https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.20270).
ranked.risks: SWE-bench-based: amd64 images, short tasks, contaminated source. The official runner is Inspect (API key); a claude -p wrapper is needed.
ranked.pilot_subset_idea: 10 paired conflicting/original instances as a side probe, not the main study.

ranked.name: METR public-tasks / hcast-public (cowthello, complex_payments)
ranked.why: Images are multi-arch amd64+arm64, and cowthello has a 5-15 h human estimate with automatic scoring (https://github.com/METR/public-tasks; https://hub.docker.com/r/metrevals/public-tasks/tags).
ranked.risks: The Inspect bridge means API keys, so a custom claude -p adapter is required. Only 1-2 public tasks are genuinely long; hcast-public tasks are 95 human-minutes or less and near ceiling for Opus 4.6 (METR runs.jsonl). clone_game needs manual scoring.
ranked.pilot_subset_idea: cowthello and complex_payments as an arm64-native supplement.

ranked.name: RepoMod-Bench (Modelcode-ai)
ranked.why: Hidden black-box tests and a Claude Code-native runner (https://github.com/Modelcode-ai/mcode-benchmark; https://arxiv.org/html/2602.22518v1).
ranked.risks: Only 21 repos. Pass rate collapses above 50k LOC, so there is a floor risk. Subscription auth is unknown and architecture is unknown.

ranked.name: Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1
ranked.why: Same Harbor pipeline as TB4, with an 8 h timeout and hidden tests; 32 tasks are in the 1-8 h band (https://github.com/harbor-framework/terminal-bench-science; https://www.tbench.ai/news/terminal-bench-science-0-1).
ranked.risks: Skewed hard (Opus 5 tops at 30%) and domain-specific. 11 tasks need 16 GB. arm64 is unknown. Use only as a reserve pool.
ranked.pilot_subset_idea: The 1-8 h, ≤8 GB tasks, if TB4 runs out.

ranked.name: SlopCodeBench
ranked.why: Its checkpointed spec sequence is a natural fit for interrupt/resume, it has hidden black-box tests, and it has a claude_code agent (https://github.com/SprocketLab/slop-code-bench; https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.24755).
ranked.risks: The README explicitly requires an Anthropic API key rather than a subscription (verified). Strict solve rates are low (Opus 4.6 17.2%), so there is a floor risk.

ranked.name: Multi-SWE-bench (hard subset)
ranked.why: Per-instance human-time buckets: there are 608 non-Python tasks labeled 1 h or more. It has hidden tests and a Harbor adapter (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2504.02605; https://github.com/harbor-framework/harbor/tree/main/adapters/multi-swe-bench).
ranked.risks: Images are amd64. Tasks are still issue-sized. It has been public since 2025, and there are no Claude 5.x baselines.
ranked.pilot_subset_idea: Hard Go/TS tasks with more than 300 changed lines.

ranked.name: SWE-EVO
ranked.why: Release-sized changes (about 610 lines across 21 files) with hidden F2P/P2P tests and a partial Fix Rate (https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.18470).
ranked.risks: There is no Claude Code harness (OpenHands/SWE-agent only, https://github.com/SWE-EVO/SWE-EVO). It is SWE-bench-style amd64, has 48 tasks, uses public history, and has no Claude baselines.

ranked.name: MLE-bench Lite
ranked.why: Long ML engineering work with hidden held-out grading and a natural premature-stop mode (https://github.com/openai/mle-bench).
ranked.risks: The base image is built for amd64 (about 25 GB). It needs Kaggle credentials (not a model key). No human times. The reference budget is 24 h on a GPU.

ranked.name: ABC-Bench (OpenMOSS)
ranked.why: Environment setup and deployment tasks, a known source of false 'done' claims. A Harbor adapter exists (https://huggingface.co/papers/2601.11077).
ranked.risks: Barely researched: duration, architecture and baselines are unknown.

ranked.name: DevOps-Gym (Harbor adapter)
ranked.why: Hidden tests, a Harbor adapter, and Java/Go build and ops work (https://github.com/harbor-framework/harbor/tree/main/adapters/devopsgym).
ranked.risks: Durations and architecture are unknown, and it is weakly long-horizon.

ranked.name: ML-Dev-Bench (Harbor adapter)
ranked.why: Hidden validators, Harbor claude-code support, binary scoring (https://github.com/laude-institute/harbor/tree/main/adapters/ml_dev_bench).
ranked.risks: No time estimates. GPU and WandB needs are unknown.

ranked.name: MLGym-Bench CPU subset (Harbor adapter)
ranked.why: Six CPU-only tasks with automatic continuous metrics (https://github.com/laude-institute/harbor/tree/main/adapters/mlgym-bench).
ranked.risks: Moderate length; mainly a pipeline check.

ranked.name: SWE-Marathon
ranked.why: Its failure taxonomy (premature termination, poor self-verification, reward hacking) is exactly on target (https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.07682), and it is on Harbor Hub.
ranked.risks: Human estimates are 40-400 h and agent limits 2-10 h. Some tasks need a GPU, Tinker or 32 GB. No configuration exceeds 30%. Too long for the 30-90 min budget.
ranked.pilot_subset_idea: At most 1-2 CPU tasks as a stress test.

ranked.name: ProgramBench (Meta)
ranked.why: Hidden fuzzed behavioral tests with partial pass rates, plus a Harbor claude-code config (https://github.com/facebookresearch/ProgramBench).
ranked.risks: The maintainers say not to run it on macOS: images are amd64-only and QEMU is slow (docs README). Resolved rate is near 0%. 6 h runs cost $10-50 each.

ranked.name: SWE-bench Pro (V1 public, V2 public, HARD-51)
ranked.why: Hidden tests and ready Claude Code tooling (locked_claude_code), but near ceiling. On the labs.scale.com HARD tab, Claude Code scores 98.0 with Opus 5 and 88.2 with Sonnet 5 (https://labs.scale.com/leaderboard/swe_bench_pro_public_v2?tab=hard). This does not contradict the V2 README's definition of HARD-51 as tasks failed by at least 2 of 5 families under the locked mini-swe-agent protocol (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/scaleapi/SWE-bench_Pro-os/main/v2/README.md); the harness makes the difference.
ranked.risks: Images are amd64-only. The locked protocol uses no-network, which fails on Docker Desktop (Harbor #2593/#2527). The budget is 50 min. Git-history leakage is documented in v1.

ranked.name: SWE-bench Verified (incl. 45 tasks ≥1 h)
ranked.why: Short (about 90% under 1 h), contaminated, and near ceiling (https://openai.com/index/why-we-no-longer-evaluate-swe-bench-verified/; https://epoch.ai/blog/what-skills-does-swe-bench-verified-evaluate). This explains the earlier null results.

ranked.name: FeatBench (TsinghuaISE)
ranked.why: Medium tasks (about 162 lines across 2.4 files) with hidden tests (https://arxiv.org/html/2509.22237v2). It mostly measures overreach and regressions.

ranked.name: SWE-Lancer / Diamond

ranking.combination_idea:
Use one runner for every arm: stock Harbor 0.24 with the claude-code agent on the subscription token (CLAUDE_FORCE_OAUTH=1 + CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN). Both arms get identical model, effort and timeout multiplier, and the treatment arm adds only `--skill .claude/skills/horizon`. Score from jobs/<job>/<trial>/ on disk.

Pilot: 10 Terminal-Bench 4.0 tasks × 2 arms. Choose them only after `-a oracle --force-build` passes natively on the M4. Mix Software, ML and Operations tasks with 2-8 h expert estimates and a 90-120 min cap.

Stage 2 (30-50 tasks): add DeepSWE Python tasks that rebuild natively on arm64. Edit their network mode to public and disallow WebFetch/WebSearch. Their pass fractions add a partial-credit SWE signal that raises statistical power.

Optionally run 10 LHTB tasks under emulation. LHTB's continue-until-timeout fork reruns plain Claude Code with hidden-verifier rejections, which makes it a perfect-gate ceiling arm. Report what share of the gap between plain single-shot and that ceiling horizon's self-written gate closes. That is the cleanest test of the gate mechanism.

Primary metrics:
- Verifier reward or pass fraction.
- False done: the final message claims success while the hidden reward is below 1 (the OverclaimBench definition). Validate the claim classifier on METR MALT, not with an LLM judge.
- Tokens and wall time.

Analysis: binary rewards at n=10 detect only very large effects (METR could not separate Claude Code from ReAct). Use paired tests (McNemar or sign test), and run 2 attempts per task-arm if usage allows.

Interruption bonus: wrap a task as Harbor multi-step, or use a small custom agent that sends SIGTERM to claude at T/2 and relaunches it with `--resume`. Apply it identically to both arms.

A 10-pair ImpossibleBench side probe can test whether horizon's mandatory gate leads to honest failure reports or to test tampering.

Fix: a bundle with real files, containing the whole harness/ package, plus python3 >= 3.10 in the image.

BLOCKING BY DESIGN: horizon's SKILL.md description only triggers on an explicit request ('explicitly requested bounded work', 'Create one when the user requests bounded continuation or invokes /horizon'). TB4 instructions never ask for it, so with `--skill` alone the treatment arm is likely the same as the baseline. The treatment must invoke horizon explicitly, via an instruction template or `--ak append_system_prompt=...`. That makes the arms differ in prompt, so the design should use a matched no-skill control prompt.

The official TB4 dataset (`-d terminal-bench/terminal-bench@4.0.0`, used by Snorkel) ships linux/amd64-only prebuilt images, so it runs under emulation on an M4. Native arm64 needs `-p tasks/<t>` from a git checkout, with unpinned base images. Each task must pass the oracle on the M4 first, because arm64 failures look exactly like agent failures (harbor#2758, tb#1601). The results will not be comparable to the leaderboard.

Exclusions on this hardware: 5 amd64-only tasks (#1802-#1806), 3 that need an H100, 9 that need 16 GB or more, 2 that need 16 CPUs, and 2 whose verifier is no-network (blocked on macOS per harbor#2593, fix PR #2594 still open). A static filter leaves about 39 candidates, enough for a pilot but not for 50 tasks.

Run length vs budget: every task has an 8 h agent timeout, and Sonnet 5.5's mean is 1h22m on Vals (a different harness). Many trials will run past the 30-90 min window, and capping the timeout changes the benchmark. With n_concurrent=1, 20 trials is about 28 h of wall time and 100 trials about 6 days.

Subscription usage: Sonnet 5.5 under Claude Code used 19.4B tokens on Snorkel's full run (2.4x Opus 5.5). A 5-hour or weekly limit hit mid-trial ends the agent run and gets scored like a failure. Detect and exclude or rerun those trials, otherwise one arm's extra token use (horizon's reviewer subagent, checkpoints) biases the comparison.

Scoring integrity: the 'hidden' tests and solutions are public on GitHub, the agent's network is public, and tb#2086 lists open reward-hacking vectors for many tasks. A gate-driven arm may game verifiers more, so audit trajectories, and consider disable_web_search, although that does not block curl.
verified.overall: TB4 is still a good benchmark for the horizon question. Its tasks are long (1-8 h expert estimates), scoring is binary and hidden in a separate verifier, and the overall baseline is mid-range (Claude Code + Sonnet 5.5 at 61.8% on Snorkel). Subscription auth through Harbor works as the ranker says. But the ranker's 'treatment arm is just --skill .claude/skills/horizon' is wrong on two counts. The skill's scripts are symlinks into the repo's harness/ package and arrive dangling in the container. And the skill's description only fires on explicit requests, which TB4 instructions never make. The other corrections: the leaderboard dataset uses amd64-only prebuilt images, so native arm64 means source builds that must each pass the oracle on the M4. Two tasks' no-network verifiers may fail on macOS Harbor. python3 is missing on several tasks. Solutions were public before Sonnet 5.5's June 2026 training cutoff, not only since July. Fix list: ship a self-contained horizon bundle; invoke it explicitly with a matched control prompt; pin Claude Code 2.1.293 and CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_OUTPUT_TOKENS=128000; filter to the ~39 runnable tasks; oracle-validate them on the M4; take a 1-trial baseline pilot to drop tasks that always pass or always fail; and detect usage-limit aborts. With all that done, it is a viable choice. Expect low statistical power at n=10 per arm, and plan for 8 h tails.

2. **Network.** Both runners are blocked on network handling in different ways. Stock Harbor cannot enforce no-network or an allowlist on Docker Desktop, so the network has to be public. Two further confounds:
- Only committed work is graded (git diff base..HEAD). If horizon's checkpoints make commits, it could win simply because the baseline forgot to commit.
- Harbor has no way to pause and resume a trial, so the forced-interruption test would need custom tooling.

If you pursue it anyway:
- Try Pier with the OAuth token and its proxy allowlist before Harbor with public network.
- Pick about 10 hard tasks from trials.json (Python and Go first, no vitest, none of the known-broken ones).
- Rebuild both images natively, point each tests/Dockerfile at the local build, and require the reference solution to score 1 and a no-op patch to score 0 on the Mac before any agent runs.
- Score with the f2p fraction gated on p2p, not the 'partial' field.
- Scan every model.patch for test-infrastructure edits.
- Run at xhigh effort or below.
- Block GitHub at the host firewall if you can.

LHTB looks right on paper but does not fit this setup. The main problem is that Harbor runs Claude Code inside the task container, which needs internet access, and on an M4 with emulated images that can't be provided for half the tasks.

**What holds up (from primary sources):**
- Hidden tests and dense partial-credit graders.
- Apache-2.0 licence.
- No grader uses an LLM API key.
- LFS is a non-issue: only reference videos under solution/.
- 39 of 47 tasks fall in the 1-8 h band, though these are author estimates.
- A uniform 90-minute cap is a single line of config (`override_timeout_sec: 5400`), already used by LHTB's own example configs. The ranker's "only multipliers" premise is wrong.
- Harbor's claude-code agent supports OAuth via CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN and can inject skills.

**What breaks:**
- **Network:** 24 of 47 tasks deny the agent container internet access. Claude Code cannot install or reach api.anthropic.com there. In stock Harbor 0.24.0 the sidecar that enforces those policies fails on Apple Silicon with amd64 images (open PR #2794). Every one of the 47 images is amd64-only.
- **Runnable subset:** the ~20 tasks left are all continue-until-timeout tasks, mostly audit/regression tasks with acknowledged, partly unfixed grader-spec defects (issues #2 and #26). The hidden tests and solutions are public on GitHub, so public-network runs need contamination audits.
- **Oracle:** the Daytona sweep scored below about 0.95, errored, or was missing on roughly 17 of the 47 tasks. Only 3 tasks have been validated on Apple Silicon.
- **Published baselines:** they come from Terminus-2, older task versions, pre-hardening verifiers (one audited sweep had 14 of 17 perfect scores from reading the grader), and a fork mode that passes scalar reward or failure text back to the agent. They are not a usable reference.
- **Ceiling arm:** the "binary perfect-gate ceiling" plan does not work with Claude Code. The fork's binary-only mode needs a resume hook that its claude_code agent lacks.
- **Interruption/resume:** there is no native support; it would need custom multi-step wrappers.

**If you still want to use it:** limit the pilot to roughly 8-10 public-network tasks with oracle 1.0, avoiding the schema-ambiguous audits (e.g. alp, foldseek, unison, su2, gdal, dicom, matpower, modflow, spice, great-expectations). Then:
- run `-a oracle` on each one locally first;
- set `disable_web_search=true` and audit trajectories for github.com/zli12321 fetches;
- use `override_timeout_sec: 5400`;
- expect to patch Harbor (PR #2794) before trying any no-network task.

That is a narrow, fragile pilot, not the benchmark's headline 46 tasks. Ranked against alternatives, I would class LHTB as conditional or not recommended for this setup.
